I am 35 years old. I never went to school, so I cannot read or write, but I know my land the way my mother knew it. My family has about 6 mu of flat land here in Quzhou. My husband works part-time at a construction site in the county town, so most days I am the one watching the fields, feeding the animals, and deciding what to do.

It is early spring now, and the wheat I sowed last October is starting to turn green. Around here, we all grow winter wheat and then summer corn on the same piece of land. That is the only way that makes sense — if you only plant one crop, you are wasting half the year, and the grain buyers only come reliably for wheat and corn. I thought about cotton because my aunt used to grow it, but cotton needs spraying every few days and picking by hand. I do not have enough hands for that with my two children in school and my husband away. Wheat and corn can be harvested by machine, and I can sell them right at the village collection point.

For wheat seeds, I buy the improved variety from Lao Zhang's shop in the township — the one with the red bag that does not fall over in wind. For corn, I buy hybrid seeds because they grow fast and strong, and we only have about 100 days between wheat harvest and the autumn frost. If the corn grows slowly, it will freeze before the kernels harden.

I rotary till the land before planting wheat every autumn. For corn, there is no time to till after wheat harvest — we have to sow within four or five days or the corn will not mature before winter. My cousin has a no-till planter, so I hire him to plant the corn straight into the wheat stubble. That is what everyone does now.

For fertilizer, I apply what I can afford and what I used last year. Last year I put down about 100 jin of compound fertilizer per mu for wheat, and the yield was good, so I will do the same. That is about 50 kg per mu. I also topdress with urea twice — once when the wheat turns green in spring, and once before heading. For corn, I put some fertilizer down at planting and side-dress once more when it is knee-high. I would rather apply a little too much than too little. A bad year means borrowing money from relatives.

I irrigate the wheat four times. The water pump costs electricity, but wheat cannot dry out, especially at heading. Corn needs less water, so two times is enough if the summer rain comes. I spray pesticides about four times for each crop, when I see insects or when the neighbors start spraying. You cannot be lazy about spraying, or the bugs and weeds will eat everything before you realize.

I expect about 500 kg per mu for wheat and a bit more for corn, maybe 530 kg, if the weather is normal like last year.
